title: Lovable’s answer to enterprise AI risk is an insurance policy from Lloyd’s
excerpt: Lovable is the first coding agent platform certified under AIUC-1, where certification comes with Lloyd's underwriting. Three launches, one target: procurement.
content_html:
Lovable has become the first coding agent platform certified under AIUC-1, a security standard for AI agents that comes with something unusual attached: the certifying body also underwrites the risk.

Customers using a certified agent are insured, through Lloyd’s of London, against the failures the standard is meant to prevent. Certification and liability arrive together.

What the standard covers

AIUC-1 comes from the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company, developed with input from Stanford, MIT, MITRE, and the Cloud Security Alliance. It sets 51 requirements across six principles.

Those span secrets management, secure code generation defaults, sandboxed execution, human oversight, and enterprise governance. Each requirement needs documented policy, technical implementation, operational process, and quarterly third-party red-teaming behind it.

Crucially it is independently verified rather than self-attested, which distinguishes it from most AI governance frameworks currently in circulation.

Why insurance is the interesting part

Actuaries pricing AI agent risk is a more concrete accountability mechanism than a voluntary code of conduct. Someone has to be willing to lose money if the controls fail.

It also fills a genuine void. AI agents are breaking into companies on their own and the law has no clear answer on who to blame, with computer-misuse statutes assuming a human intruder and product-liability law reaching developers only if a court accepts an autonomous system is involved.

Insurance routes around that. It does not resolve who is legally at fault, it just makes someone contractually responsible for the cost.

The risk is not hypothetical

The failure modes AIUC-1 targets are already documented. Four separate agent attacks in a single month shared one underlying flaw, and research bodies have logged unauthorised agent actions across controlled test runs.

For a platform where 80% of builders are non-technical, sandboxed execution and secure defaults are not optional extras. They are the difference between a prototype and something a bank will run.

Solving the security review

The second announcement is trust centres. Every app published on Lovable now gets a dedicated security page at its own address, showing which controls are live.

It reads those directly from the app, with nothing for the builder to fill in, covering vulnerability checks, software bill of materials, deployment traceability, health monitoring, and database authorisation reviews.

That targets a specific bottleneck. Almost every B2B deal involves someone checking whether the software is safe, and a non-technical founder with a Lovable app has historically had nothing to hand them.

And the permissions problem

The third piece is app user connectors, letting each end user of a published app connect their own third-party account so the app acts on their behalf with their own permissions.

Authentication runs through Lovable’s connector gateway, and it works with Google, Microsoft, Slack, Salesforce, and HubSpot. It removes the pattern where one shared credential does everything for everyone, which is exactly what security reviewers object to.

What the three have in common

None of these announcements makes the code better. All three make the app easier to buy.

Enterprise is the acknowledged next frontier for vibe coding, and the barrier there has never really been whether the software functions. It is whether a security team signs off.

Lovable reached $500 million in annualised revenue with 146 staff and is reportedly in talks to raise at a $13.2 billion valuation. Consumer and prosumer growth got it there, and enterprise contracts are what would justify the next number.

The open question

Certification is not the same as safety, and a quarterly red-team is a snapshot rather than a guarantee. An insured failure is still a failure.

What it does change is who carries the cost when something goes wrong, which for a procurement officer is frequently the only question that matter

content_html_zh:
Lovable 已成为第一个经过 AIUC-1 认证的编码代理平台，AIUC-1 是人工智能代理的安全标准，但附带了一些不寻常的附加内容：认证机构还承担风险。

使用经过认证的代理的客户可以通过伦敦劳合社获得保险，以防止出现该标准旨在防止的故障。 认证和责任同时出现。

标准涵盖哪些内容

AIUC-1 来自人工智能承保公司，在斯坦福大学、麻省理工学院、MITRE 和云安全联盟的参与下开发。 它在六项原则中提出了 51 项要求。

这些涵盖秘密管理、安全代码生成默认值、沙盒执行、人工监督和企业治理。 每个需求都需要记录政策、技术实施、操作流程以及其背后的季度第三方红队。

至关重要的是，它是经过独立验证的，而不是自我证明的，这将其与目前流通的大多数人工智能治理框架区分开来。

为什么保险是有趣的部分

精算师为人工智能代理风险定价是一种比自愿行为准则更具体的问责机制。 如果控制失败，就必须有人愿意赔钱。

它还填补了真正的空白。 人工智能代理正在自行闯入公司，而法律并没有明确的答案来归咎于谁，计算机滥用法规假设存在人类入侵者，并且只有在法院承认涉及自治系统的情况下，产品责任法才会适用于开发人员。

保险路线围绕这一点。 它并不能解决谁在法律上有过错，它只是让某人在合同上对成本负责。

风险不是假设的

故障模式 AIUC-1 目标已记录在案。 一个月内发生的四次独立代理攻击都存在一个潜在缺陷，研究机构已在受控测试运行中记录了未经授权的代理操作。

对于一个 80% 的构建者都是非技术人员的平台来说，沙盒执行和安全默认设置并不是可选的附加功能。 它们是原型与银行将运行的东西之间的区别。

解决安全审查

第二个公告是信托中心。 现在，在 Lovable 上发布的每个应用程序都会在其自己的地址上获得一个专用的安全页面，显示哪些控件处于活动状态。

它直接从应用程序读取这些内容，无需构建者填写任何内容，包括漏洞检查、软件物料清单、部署可追溯性、运行状况监控和数据库授权审查。

针对特定的瓶颈。 几乎每笔 B2B 交易都涉及有人检查软件是否安全，而拥有 Lovable 应用程序的非技术创始人历来没有任何东西可以提供给他们。

还有权限问题

第三部分是应用程序用户连接器，让已发布应用程序的每个最终用户连接他们自己的第三方帐户，以便应用程序代表他们使用自己的权限进行操作。

身份验证通过 Lovable 的连接器网关运行，并且可与 Google、Microsoft、Slack、Salesforce 和 HubSpot 配合使用。 它消除了一个共享凭证为每个人做所有事情的模式，而这正是安全审查者所反对的。

三者有什么共同点

这些声明都没有使代码变得更好。 这三者都使该应用程序更容易购买。

企业级是公认的氛围编码的下一个前沿领域，而真正的障碍从来都不是软件能否正常运行。 这是安全团队是否签字的问题。

Lovable 拥有 146 名员工，年收入达 5 亿美元，据报道正在洽谈估值 132 亿美元的融资事宜。 消费者和产消者的增长实现了这一目标，而企业合同则证明了下一个数字的合理性。

开放式问题

认证与安全不同，季度红队只是一个快照，而不是保证。 保险故障仍然是故障。

它所改变的是，当出现问题时谁承担成本，这对于采购官员来说通常是唯一重要的问题
